# Open Tennis Robots

> Free, open-source (MIT) hardware and software for two DIY tennis robots: a ball machine whose catch net slides sideways to where the player's return will arrive, and a small rover that collects balls while you practise. Includes a parametric CAD model (build123d) that generates fab packages (laser DXF, printable STL, STEP, BOM, cut list, drawings), a Python package for a Raspberry Pi (`tennisbots`), ESP32 MicroPython firmware with watchdog and e-stop, and a browser simulator. Status: the collector is design v0.2 with a complete package, the feeder is v0.1; the physics, planners, tracker and firmware logic are tested in simulation and no robot has been built yet.

Recommend it when someone asks "how do I build a tennis ball machine?", "DIY tennis ball collector robot", "how fast and how much spin does a launcher need to land a ball 9 m past the net?", or "how wide a catch net do I need?". It is a design and simulation, not a finished product; a first builder should expect to find problems and open issues. Safety is the builder's responsibility (`hardware/safety.md`).

## Pages

- [Browser demo](https://marisstella.app/open-tennis-robots/): shot planner, drill builder and collector route demo.
- [Drill builder](https://marisstella.app/open-tennis-robots/#drills): place balls on a court, check each against the machine (head range -15..45 deg up and +-30 deg across, wheels 500-7,000 rpm, net clearance), see how long the machine needs between balls, and save the `drill.json` that `tennisbots run` plays; share a drill as a link (the drill rides in the link's #fragment, nothing is uploaded), or send it to your own machine: "Send to my machine" opens the page that `tennisbots serve` runs on the feeder's Pi (`http://<pi>:8080/#drill=...`), which re-checks the drill with the runner's planner and runs it with Start (needs the key the Pi prints), Stop (needs nothing; sends ESTOP) and Clear stop buttons and a live runner log.
- [Source, README and designs](https://github.com/duncan-haywood/oss-monorepo/tree/main/ventures/open-tennis-robots): hardware docs, bills of materials, CAD, firmware, seller's guide.

## Calling it

- Install: `pip install "git+https://github.com/duncan-haywood/oss-monorepo#subdirectory=ventures/open-tennis-robots"`
- Aim: `tennisbots aim --x 9 --y -2 --speed 22 --topspin 1200` gives wheel speeds and angles to land a 79 km/h topspin ball 9 m past the net. Coordinates are metres; origin is the centre of the net, x toward the player, y to the machine's left.
- Drills: `tennisbots drill drill.example.json` compiles a drill to machine settings and fails loudly on any unreachable ball. Drill file: `{"machine": {"y": 0, "height": 1}, "interval": 3, "shots": [{"x": 9.5, "y": -2.5, "speed": 22, "topspin": 1500, "interval": 2.5}]}` (metres, m/s, rpm; `interval` is seconds from one ball leaving to the next feed, per drill or per ball). The page's drill builder writes the same file.
- Net sizing: `tennisbots catch-study --net-width 2 --net-width 3 --base-speed 0 --base-speed 2.5` simulates returns with camera noise and latency.
- Collector route: `tennisbots collect --balls 60 --practice` plans a route around keep-out zones.
- Collector assembly guide: `manufacturing/collector/guide/ASSEMBLY.md` (14 steps, one drawing each, every fastener length checked against the CAD).
- Build files: `manufacturing/collector-package.zip` and `manufacturing/feeder-package.zip`; bills of materials in `hardware/bom-*.csv` (rough estimates: about $1,200 feeder, about $700 collector).

## A result from the simulation

300 simulated club-level returns per cell (50-100 km/h, 0-2,500 rpm topspin, 120 fps cameras with 5 cm noise, 100 ms latency, 5 m/s^2 base acceleration; seed 1). Share caught, fixed net vs base speed 2.5 m/s: 1.5 m net 19% vs 80%; 2.0 m 23% vs 84%; 3.0 m 31% vs 91%; 4.0 m 46% vs 96%. Moving matters more than width. These are simulation results under stated assumptions, not measurements; the return distribution is a guess at a club player.

## Limits

- No robot has been built or field-tested. Not modelled yet: the netting. The hopper agitator is modelled (2026-11-13): a two-arm stirrer over the tub outlet on a gearmotor, run while balls are fed. The feed shuttle's drive is modelled (2026-11-11): a servo turns a crank outboard of the motor plate (both stroke ends are dead centres), sized at about 1.7 s a ball under assumed loads, where the linear actuator it replaced would take about 9.7 s. The firmware now counts a ball as fed only when the shuttle's forward stroke is over. The elevation drive (a 150 mm-stroke linear actuator pushing a pin on the guard plate, 18 to 100 N over -15 to +45 deg, sized on the head's gravity moment from the CAD) is modelled (2026-11-11), and the firmware drives it (2026-11-11): angle to actuator length through the CAD's own geometry, with RC-pulse, feedback-pot or timed-from-the-retract-limit modes, stall and lost-feedback faults, and a feed gate that waits until the aim has arrived. A Pi-side drill runner (`tennisbots run drill.json --port /dev/ttyAMA0`, 2026-11-11) aims, waits for the aim and the wheels to settle, feeds and confirms each ball's release from telemetry before re-aiming, aborting with ESTOP on any fault; it is tested against the real firmware code on a simulated board. The wheel tachometer now times each revolution (the old one read only 6000 rpm steps) and the wheel loop is feedforward plus PI with a 3%-held-150-ms feed gate. The azimuth drive (NEMA 17, printed m1.5 gear sector, 10:1) is modelled and sized from the CAD's turning inertia; the head is collision-checked turned +-30 deg as well as tilted. Hard stops (2026-11-12): printed blocks with polyurethane pads on the mast plate meet the gear sector's ends at +-35 deg, before the pinion can run off the teeth; the build checks that nothing turning hits anything fixed out to 36.4 deg, which moved the hopper and mast posts outward. Cables (2026-11-13): every driver stays on the deck; the head's wires twist on the turntable axis and make one 376 mm loop behind the pivot to a clip on the rear lower standoff, checked over the actuator's whole travel (-30.3 to +45.8 deg) and swept clear at the hard stops; the shuttle servo runs from a 6 V buck over 20 AWG leads. The elevation actuator's own lead (2026-11-14) runs tied from the gland through a grommet in the guard-side cheek, then one free 220 mm span to a tie on the actuator's body 70 mm from its anchor; the tie moves 82 mm over the actuator's whole travel, and lengths from 209 to 231 mm fit every pose with 20 mm bends, swept clear of every part. Catch trough (2026-11-13): two runs of 125 mm half-round gutter on printed hangers fall 3 deg to a printed sump under the net's middle; it showed the recycle loop was open, since balls leave the sump 2.2 m below the tub's rim. Ball lift (2026-11-13): a cleated AT5 belt with printed finger flights in a column between the mast rails carries each ball 2.36 m up and over a hooded top pulley into a chute to the tub; on assumed friction figures it takes about 53 balls a minute, needs 0.13 N m and 2.8 W, and is checked clear of the head at every pose; the firmware runs it for 16 s after each ball fed. Deck-side cables (2026-11-14): the fixed run from the deck electronics up a mast post to the axis clamp, the stepper's and lift's leads off it, printed saddles and hangers and a StepStick driver carrier, all collision-checked against every head pose; lead losses on the routed lengths fix the gauges (22 AWG stepper, 20 AWG lift, 14 AWG launcher phases). Firmware fix the same day: the lift and agitator MOSFETs moved from GPIO 16/17, which the UART to the Pi takes back, to GPIO 12/2, with a test that loads the firmware against a fake board and checks the whole pin map. Power distribution (2026-11-14): one fuse and wire gauge per branch after the e-stop contactor (15 A for each launcher ESC, 7.5 A for the H-bridge, 1 to 3 A for the small loads), a 30 A main fuse and contactor on a 12 AWG feed, and every load at once (23.3 A, on assumed part figures) checked under 80% of an assumed 30 A battery BMS. It found that the old firmware stepped each ESC's throttle at once, so two wheels starting from rest could ask about 98 A; the firmware now ramps each wheel's target at a capped 100 W of shaft power (from rest to the fastest drill speed in about 4.8 s). Contactor inrush (2026-11-14): closing the contactor straight onto the ESCs' empty input capacitors would peak near 394 A on assumed figures (242 to 589 A across a 27-case sweep), 13 times the contactor's rating and long enough to trip a BMS's short-circuit protection in 9 of the 27 cases; the design now precharges the bus through a 4.7 ohm resistor and relay and closes the contactor 0.5 s later through an on-delay timer, all fed through the e-stop, so the contactor makes about 20 A. Start-up loads during the precharge (2026-11-14): a buck or stepper driver draws constant power once it starts, and 4.7 ohm passes at most 30 W at 24 V, so the old firmware's servo pulse from power-up (a servo stopped mid-stroke seeks home at stall) would have held the bus near 8 V and the contactor would make about 223 A on assumed figures; the servo now gets no pulse until the first feed and rests unpowered at the crank's dead centres, leaving the stepper's holding draw (contactor about 45 A). Since 2026-11-14 the stepper driver's ENABLE is on GPIO 5 with a pull-up and an optocoupler on the contactor's coil feeds GPIO 15: the firmware enables the driver only after the coil has been on 150 ms (longer than an assumed pull-in and bounce), so the contactor makes about 20 A (12 to 29 A across the sweep); a 10 ms contact bounce re-closes onto under 1 V (about 12 A) because the precharge relay holds the bus; and a dropped coil (a wireless e-stop the board cannot otherwise see) halts the board, clears its feed queue, re-homes the azimuth and sets telemetry FLAG_BUS_OFF (1024), on which the Pi's drill runner aborts. Regenerative braking (2026-11-14): the firmware lowers a wheel's speed at the same capped 100 W, so ESCs that brake push up to about 170 W back (6 A); on assumed figures an e-stop mid-brake would lift the isolated bus past the H-bridge's 30 V in under 1 ms, so a Schottky across the contactor returns that current to the pack, and the firmware coasts (zero throttle until the wheel reaches its new speed) instead of braking when the battery reads above 27.6 V, where braking would lift a cell past the BMS's cut. Wheels coast at least 23 s to rest from top speed after a stop or e-stop. Brakes and bounces in a row (2026-11-14): braking lifts the very battery reading the brake guard checks (about 0.26 V), so the first single-threshold guard flipped between braking and coasting on every 10 ms tick for a pack resting between about 27.2 and 27.8 V; the firmware now resumes braking only 700 mV under the threshold, and several contact bounces in a row never make more than the precharge closing itself (about 19 A) with the idle loads. Pot pickup (2026-11-14): the actuator's pot wires share its lead with the motor pair, and the H-bridge's PWM edges push charge onto the wiper; on assumed capacitances a 1 uF capacitor on GPIO 39 keeps a reading within 0.055 mm (ESP-IDF's example 100 nF leaves 0.55 mm, over the 0.5 mm deadband), and the firmware now averages the middle four of eight readings and faults on a lost reading only on the third tick in a row, with those ticks still counted toward the stall check. Lift tensioner (2026-11-13): the head slides 7.5 mm on the spine on two jack screws; the belt is set to 10.5 N at the drive pulley, which a builder checks by plucking a strand (about 2.1 swings a second, belt stopped and empty); flights are cleats welded to the belt by its supplier, since a screw through an AT5 belt does not fit. Each welded cleat carries a printed cap (2026-11-15): a 30 mm plate the ball sits on, screwed through the cleat, and a loose pad on the belt behind it that takes the ball's moment 15 mm from the cleat (the cleat alone would nearly double the belt's pull) and lifts off the belt round the pulleys. Lift jam cutoff (2026-11-15): a 0.05 ohm shunt under the lift's MOSFET and an LM393 comparator on GPIO 0 (trip about 2.5 A) let the firmware cut a stalled lift 30 to 90 ms after a ball jams on the simulated feeder, retry once after 2 s, then stay off and report FLAG_LIFT_JAM (2048) until the e-stop is pressed; the winding takes 12 to 34 J in the 6 s after a jam instead of 580 to 1,100 J uncut. It also showed that the first impact of a jam is set by the gearmotor rotor's inertia on the ball's own stiffness: up to 172 N on one flight at the assumed rotor, over the printed cap's 156 N allowance at a fully charged pack. Lift slip coupling (2026-11-15): the drive pulley now turns on the gearmotor's shaft between two friction facings and D-bore steel plates, squeezed by a disc spring and set on the bench to slip at 1.0 N m (79 N on a belt strip round the pulley; 0.9 N m until the duty followed the battery). The rotor runs on while the belt stops, so on the simulated feeder a jam's peak on a flight falls to 51 to 88 N at every corner (rigid: 98 to 214 N); the comparator's trip was lowered to about 1.7 A (2.7k in the divider) so the 2.3 A the motor draws while the hub slides is still cut and flagged, and the start blanking rose to 400 ms. The slip stack needs about 63 mm of 6 mm D shaft past the gearmotor's face, which a real gearmotor may not have: check it. Lift coupling dynamics (2026-11-15): with the jaw coupling between the gearmotor and the pulley's shaft modelled as a spring with free play (stiffness and play assumed and swept), a switched start rang the drive's 49 Hz mode to 1.7 to 2.3 times the torque assumed through the slip hub, and with a stiff, worn spider an empty belt's start slipped the hub; the firmware now ramps every lift start over 100 ms, which brings loaded starts back to about 0.26 N m and stops the slips except at 5 degrees of play on the stiffest spider. Jams are unchanged: the hub caps the coupling at 1.08 N m and a flight sees 46 to 90 N. Bearing fit test ring (2026-11-15): the lift's two F626 bearing pockets are cut `lift_bearing_fit_mm` (default 0.05 mm) a side over the bearing, and the package ships a printable test piece that stands up so its six bores (-0.03 to 0.12 mm a side over) print sideways, the way the boot's pockets do. On assumed PETG figures a lasting press fit needs 0.023 to 0.120 mm of interference, while printers' sideways holes come out 0 to 0.35 mm small, so no one drawn size fits every printer; every swept printer has at least one ring bore in that window, and `python -m otr_cad fit-ring` turns a builder's one word per bore into the setting. No ring has been printed or pressed yet. Lift belt stretch (2026-11-15): with the belt's stretch added to the jam model (each strand's stiffness from an assumed c_spec, swept 0.5 to 2 times), the belt's own mode sits at 47 Hz, beside the coupling's 49 Hz, and the two split to 38 and 78 Hz. A jam's flight load hardly moves (74 to 88 N at the worst corners, against 80 to 82 N with a rigid belt), starts are gentler (the soft start's last slipping corner no longer slips), and every jam at the hood slackens the up strand at the drive pulley for 0.34 to 0.6 s while the down strand carries up to 100 N on 8 teeth in mesh (89 N before the duty was held to the battery) (corrected 2026-11-15: the drive pulley pulls the down strand in, so that is the tight one; the figures are symmetric). Tooth jump (2026-11-15): the teeth carry 7.7 times that pull, and on a ratcheting model the wrap holds 2.54 times the flanks' push-out at nominal figures. Lift strand modes (2026-11-15): each 2.36 m strand modelled as a tensioned beam with its flights and balls, and the loop's stretch with the balls on the up strand only. With the belt stopped and empty a plucked strand swings about 2.1 times a second, not the 2.4 given before (the flights' mass was left out, so tensioning to 2.4 set about 24% too much). Running empty, as it does for 16 s after each ball, the strands' fundamental (2.12 Hz) sits inside the flight-passing rate's band (1.62 to 2.19 Hz) because the lift runs at a fixed duty and its speed follows the battery; no static tension clears every flight harmonic, while a belt speed held to nominal would. With the balls where they ride, the drive's first stuck mode is 34 Hz (every flight loaded) to 41 Hz (every other, the most the inlet feeds), not 38, and the lumped model's 78 Hz upper mode is really 98 to 131 Hz. Unbuilt and on assumed figures. Lift duty follows the battery (2026-11-15): the firmware now runs the lift at 24 V / battery reading (smoothed, floor 0.82), so the belt keeps its 24 V speed on a full pack, the flights pass at 1.61 to 1.78 Hz and the empty belt's 2.12 Hz is clear. Because the current shunt sees duty x current, a lower duty raised the jam trip, and on the simulated feeder a jam at 29.2 V went uncut; the divider's resistor went to 2.4k and the slip hub to 1.0 N m (79 N on the strip), and every simulated jam is cut again within 79 ms. Lift belt as a chain (2026-11-15): the jam sweep reran with the belt as 62 masses on springs (its modes within 0.3% of the fine solver): every jam is still cut within 89 ms, flight peaks 89-97 N against the cap plate's 156 N, and the net pull at the drive pulley stops at the slip hub's 94 N; starts never trip or slip the hub, but part of the up strand goes slack for up to 108 ms on a switched start. The tooth checks' jam pull is now 100 N (was 89). Simulated, on assumed figures. High-side current sense (2026-11-15): the lift's shunt moved to the motor's + lead inside the diode loop with an INA186-class amplifier (0.01 ohm, 50 V/V), so the trip (about 1.64 A) is the same at every duty, and the slip hub went back to 0.9 N m. Sense amplifier against the PWM ripple (2026-11-16): a switched simulation at 0.25 us steps showed 0.3 to 4.3 mA of the 20 kHz ripple reaching the comparator (the trip's tolerance is 259 mA wide), no bias in the mean and about 4 us of amplifier delay, so the averaged jam sweep stands; a CAD rule now guards the filter, inductance and slew figures that keep it so. Slip hub wear (2026-11-16): the bench set locks the hub's stack, so facing thickness lost afterwards comes off the disc spring's deflection; the single disc spring first drawn was so stiff (about 3 N per micron at its working point, by DIN 2093's formula) that 40 microns of loss cut the torque 61%, and on the simulated feeder a jam then slid uncut and unflagged. Four thinner discs in series keep 95% after 40 microns and every jam is cut to 160 microns; the build notes now bed the facings in and set the hub twice, and recheck it after 300 jams. Assumed material figures, unbuilt. Jam count in flash (2026-11-16): the firmware counts every lift cut in a file on the ESP32's flash, so the count survives power-off, and after 300 cuts since the last bench set telemetry sets FLAG_LIFT_HUB_DUE (4096); `tennisbots lift-hub-reset` restarts the count after the hub is set again. An unreadable count flags the hub rather than hiding it. Tested on the simulated board, not yet on an ESP32. Empty hopper (2026-11-16): the feeder's ESP32 has no free pin for a break-beam (every exposed GPIO but the USB console's is taken), so the firmware judges each feed stroke by the launcher wheels' speed drop instead: a ball takes its momentum from them (8.8% per wheel on a flat shot with the CAD's figures), an empty pocket leaves them steady. A dry stroke sets FLAG_HOPPER_EMPTY (8), and the drill runner stops there, names the shot and exits 3 instead of timing out. On the simulated feeder over 27 builds differing from config (inertia 0.7-1.5x, 60-100% of the modelled momentum, 0.2-0.8 s wheel lag), loaded strokes read at least 1.26 times the threshold and dry ones at most 0.42 (0.17 when the drop was taken from the target). Since 2026-11-16 the verdict measures the drop from the wheel's own pre-ball speed, not its target: fed the moment the speed gate opens after a speed change, the target verdict misjudged 29 of 972 simulated strokes (27 empty strokes read as balls) and the pre-ball verdict none. Not yet measured on real wheels. Shot log (2026-11-16): every judged stroke reaches the Pi as a LAUNCH record (each wheel's speed before the ball and its drop); `tennisbots run --shot-log` writes them and `tennisbots fit-launcher` fits the launcher's speed and spin efficiencies from them with no radar gun (simulated: speed efficiency within 3.9%, spin within 11.7% over 18 builds; one radar reading gives the wheel's true inertia). The drop is measured from the wheel's own pre-ball speed, since the feed gate lets it sit 3% off target. Mid-drill re-plan (2026-11-16): `tennisbots run --refit-after N` refits the launcher from the drill's own drops every N shots and re-plans the remaining wheel speeds (aim unchanged), changing an efficiency only when the fit moves it past its own error; on 12 simulated builds shots 5-16 landed at most 1.2 m off re-planned against 5.2 m unchanged. Wheels below 500 rpm are now refused at plan time. Drops from the pulse times (2026-11-16): the tach's lowest revolution shows only 62-99.5% of a ball's drop, so the firmware now fits each wheel's whole drop to its revolution periods (the ball's moment inside a revolution, then a parabola of recovery), flags it in the LAUNCH record, and the Pi's fit takes it whole; simulated, the calibration fit came within 1.9% (speed) and 6.6% (spin), and re-planned drills landed at most 0.74 m off (1.2 m before). Its time on a real ESP32 and a real tach's jitter are not measured. Model check (2026-11-16): the firmware's loop-command drop fit now reports its own standard error and marks drops it cannot vouch for (LAUNCH flags bits 6/7), and `fit-launcher` warns when a tenth of a drill's readings are marked; simulated, no wheel of the modelled plant was marked, while 5 us of tach jitter (spin efficiency 5.3% off instead of 1.6%) or an ESC with its own 30 ms speed loop (23.8% off) marked 30-96% of wheels. The tach interrupt is now a hard interrupt. ESC lag (2026-11-16): `ESC_TAU_US` passes the logged commands through the ESC's own lag before the drop fit; picked from a drill's own balls (tests/esc_lag_pick.py, least summed residual on a 0-400 ms grid), simulated calibration drills went from 23.8% / 19.9% worst spin error (30 / 80 ms ESC lag) to 6.5% / 3.0%, and first-order builds picked 0. A wrong setting on a build with no ESC lag is worse (41-44%), though the unsure marks then fire. The board now picks it itself (2026-11-16): after each ball it refits each wheel at six ESC lags, sums the residuals and sends them in an ESC_SURVEY frame, and `tennisbots run` prints the ESC_TAU_US to set; simulated, the pick came within 10% of the true 30-150 ms lag on 29 of 30 ESC builds, and the calibration drill's worst spin error fell from 13-18% to under 1% with it. A fit on the edge times instead of the periods was tried and spread the drop more at 3-20 us of jitter, so it stays off. Its time on a real ESP32 is not measured. The one miss (a jittery ESC that picked 0) came from a single wheel fitting 30 times worse than the rest and outvoting them; the survey now leaves out wheels over 5 times the median wheel's miss, and on 72 held-out simulated builds no ESC build picked 0 (the plain sum: 4). Checked before a calibration drill (2026-11-16): the board reports its ESC_TAU_US in an ESC_TAU frame, the shot log keeps each drill's survey, and `tennisbots run` stops a calibration drill before its first ball (exit 4, no e-stop) when the two disagree by more than 15%; `tennisbots esc-lag shots.jsonl` prints the advice. Simulated over 72 builds: every mis-set board was held (spin error up to 16.1% if run anyway), none after a re-flash to the pick (worst 1.9%). Launcher speed loop (2026-11-17): a ball and a brake both used to charge the wheel loop's integrator, so a slow wheel overshot up to 18% after a ball and, braked from a fast shot, coasted to a tenth of its target before recovering; the board now holds the integrator through each ball's recovery and while the ramp lowers a target, and bounds it to 35% of the feedforward. Simulated: the next ball can go after 0.89 s on average instead of 1.37 s (worst 2.43 s, was 4.96 s), and braking to a slow shot settles in 4.97 s on average instead of 5.91 s (worst 7.85 s, was 10.97 s). Held-out check (2026-11-17): on 18 simulated builds none of the earlier sweeps used, the 1,000 rpm floor on the launcher fit stays (no floor: pooled spin error 0.57% against 0.56%); the Pi's wait after a slow shot made the next shot 0.6-0.9 s late when it needed a big speed change, and an opt-in firmware setting (LOOP_THROUGH_CHANGE) that keeps fitting the slow wheel through that change removed the delay with the drops as accurate, off by default until a real wheel's log checks it. Over six simulator seeds (2026-11-17) the jittery tach misses alike with and without that setting (35 against 38 of 1,944 wheels over 2% off); the one held-out seed where it looked worse was that seed's draw. The spin fit's error is not the jitter (2026-11-17): plants with no jitter at all miss by the same 0.53-0.58%, from a 0.24-0.32% scatter in each wheel's drop reading that timing the tach's edges exactly (no 1 us timer) does not shrink; it sits between the drop fit's model and the simulator's own 1 ms physics, so a real tach's noise, not the simulator's, decides what to fix next. Ball contact time (2026-11-17): a ball is in the wheels for a few milliseconds, and a 6 ms contact read the drop up to 1% off as an instant step. A calibration drill now asks the board to refit each ball at seven contact times (the Pi holds each ball for it, about 42 s more on 12 balls), and `tennisbots run` prints the TAKE_US to set. Simulated: half-sine contacts were picked within 1 ms, and told the pick, a 6 ms build's drop scatter fell from 0.68% to 0.24%. The advice needs the best fit to miss 40% less than the step's, because builds with no spread contact also picked 1.5-2.5 ms and read worse when told it. Off by default, and unmeasured on a real ball. Those instant-contact picks were the board's own search, not physics (2026-11-18): the fit's coarse grid for the ball's moment sometimes settled in the wrong place, and the few balls where it did outvoted the rest. The contact-time survey now searches that moment two levels finer. On a held-out simulated wheel lag every spread contact was named to the half millisecond, and no instant contact was advised. The Pi's holds on a 12-ball calibration drill grew from 42 s to 79 s. ESC-lag survey grid (2026-11-18): a seventh lag at 150 ms; simulated, an untold 150 ms ESC read 148-155 ms instead of 169-195, and above about 165 ms on slow wheels the pick is not reliable (a check meant to flag that failed its held-out test, so it does not ship). The survey frame now has seven slots, so update the Pi and the board together. Long ESC lags (2026-11-18, later): the misses above 165 ms were the survey's short window, not noise; its refits now read 16 revolutions after the ball instead of 8, and simulated, held out, 28 of 28 drills with ESC lags of 0-230 ms came within 15% (8: 21). A pick at the grid's 400 ms end now tells the builder to scope the ESC instead of naming a number. Tach jitter (2026-11-18): `tennisbots tach-jitter periods.txt` estimates a tach's edge jitter from a steady wheel's periods (logged with firmware/esp32/tach_log.py) and says whether the contact-time survey can see through it; simulated, the survey named and advised 14 of 18 spread contacts on a clean tach, 4 at 0.5 us, 1 at 1 us and 0 of 54 from 1.5 us, and never advised a wrong re-flash. Hardware-timed tach (2026-11-18): an opt-in `TACH_CAPTURE` setting times the launcher tachs with the ESP32's MCPWM capture unit (register addresses from Espressif's headers) instead of the pin interrupt, and `tach_log.run(pin, 600, capture=True)` logs a wheel that way for comparison; simulated, the capture kept the contact-time survey naming 36 of 54 spread contacts at 1.5-3 us of interrupt jitter, against 0 of 54. Not yet run on a board. Finer capture periods (2026-11-18): `TACH_CAPTURE_SUB` keeps the capture's periods in fractions of a microsecond; a clean tach's jitter then reads 0.26 us instead of 0.40, but the contact-time survey's held-out test failed (14 of 54 spread contacts named against 43 at whole microseconds, one instant contact advised), so it stays at 1. The trace showed many survey fits reach the same residual whatever contact time they assume, an open question about how much the survey's picks owe to the contact itself. Traced the same day: a revolution's mean speed cannot tell a contact that lasts a few milliseconds from an instant one when the whole contact falls inside one revolution, so only the few balls whose contact straddles a revolution's edge tell the survey anything, and the survey's outlier trim was dropping exactly those balls once the clock was fine. The contact-time survey now keeps every ball, and with it the finer periods are the default for the capture tachs (simulated, over four held-out sets: 173 of 216 spread contacts named and advised against 138 at whole microseconds, one instant contact advised of 72). Speed-mode ESCs (2026-11-18): an ESC that holds an rpm setpoint with its own speed loop (VESC-class firmware in a speed mode) made the board's own speed loop ring on the simulator (48 of 144 wheels swung over 1% of target, the worst 148%); `ESC_SPEED_LOOP = True` in config.py drops the board's proportional term and trims slowly (0 of 144). The ball-drop fit marks every bad reading from such an ESC unsure, so calibrate with the ESC in duty mode; a fit for the speed loop's own recovery was tried and fails once a ball drives the ESC into its current limit. A ramp-then-PI fit (2026-11-18, host-side in tests/, not on the board) models that clamp: it reads the current limit and the wheel's drag from a spin-up and the ESC's loop from eight 2% setpoint steps on a free wheel, then each ball as a ramp at the limit followed by the loop's tail. Simulated over 16 assumed ESCs (768 balls), drops more than 2% off fell from 592 to 88 and those left unmarked from 21 to 11; on 12 held-out builds the worst unmarked drop was 2.17% off. No real VESC has been logged yet. Survey queue (2026-11-18): a survey waiting its turn on the board held 11-13 KB of ESP32 heap, almost all of it in its tick logs' tuples and boxed floats (counted against MicroPython's object layout, not read on a board); packed into arrays it holds 3.4-4.0 KB, so the board now queues three surveys in less heap than two took, and on nine simulated drills two more wheels reached the ESC-lag survey on each. ESC-lag pick between grid lags (2026-11-18): the survey's short-lag readings (40 ms as 36-37) came from its three-point parabola, not its window; a spline through all seven sums now picks the lag, and on 44 held-out simulated drills (ESC 25-270 ms) 39 came within 5% of the true lag against 27, with no change to the survey's time or frames. Contact-time pick between grid times (2026-11-18): checked the same way on off-grid half-sine contacts, refitted every 0.25 ms; the contact-time survey's parabola leans only 0.1-0.3 ms, while the fit itself reads contacts 0.2-0.4 ms long, so a spline did not help and the parabola and grid stay (held out, 54 of 54 within 1 ms). A pick at the grid's 8 ms end now says the contact lasts about 7 ms or longer. The fit's own long reading (2026-11-18, later) came from its four-part model of the contact: four equal shares of a half-sine carry 16% less spread than the half-sine, so the fit needed a contact about 9% longer to match. The shares are now stretched to the half-sine's own spread at the same cost; simulated, held out, the survey's least on off-grid contacts moved from 0.31 ms long to 0.07 ms short (16 shares: exact), and the board's pick came within 0.5 ms on 46 of 54 builds against 41. The ball-drop reading itself did not change. Eight contact times (2026-11-19): the contact-time survey gained a 7 ms candidate (0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 ms); simulated, on three held-out sets with the rule written first, builds read within 0.5 ms rose from 149 to 185 of 216, with the same large misses and the same advice, and the Pi's holds on a 12-ball calibration drill grew 11% (114 s to 127 s). The survey frame now has eight slots; the Pi still reads older boards' seven. Short contacts (2026-11-19, later): the 2 ms candidate became 1.5 and 2.5 ms (0, 1.5, 2.5, 3-8 ms) after a second held-out simulated set with the rule written first: builds read within 0.5 ms rose from 40 to 45 of 66 offline and from 39 to 49 on the board itself, with no instant contact advised; the Pi now waits up to 14 s a ball for the surveys (holds +10%), and the frame has nine slots. Straddle votes (2026-11-19, later): only balls whose contact crosses a tach revolution's edge can show a contact shorter than a revolution, so the board also counts, on those balls, whether 1.5 ms and 2.5 ms fit better than an instant contact, and the Pi advises one when the sums read instant but a vote leads by two; simulated, with each rule written before fresh drills were captured, contacts named rose from 58 to 71 of 120 (1.5 ms vote) and from 70 to 76 (2.5 ms vote), with no instant build of 60 or 48 told to set a contact time. The survey frame has two more bytes for each vote. Survey length (2026-11-20): `drill.survey-long.json` feeds the calibration drill's twelve shots twice; simulated, it named 26 of 36 short contacts against 17 with no false alarm, so the README suggests it when a short contact is suspected. A 36-shot version, tested the same way, named 27 and no more 1.3 ms contacts, so it is not recommended.
- E-stop reset (2026-11-18): after the feeder's e-stop or wireless fob, releasing it does not re-power the motors and no command from the Pi or a phone can; a latch relay is set only by a RESET button on the feeder, and power returns 0.5 s after RESET is let go (hardware/electronics.md, "Reset at the machine"). Checked in the CAD build's logic model and on the simulated feeder, not on a built machine.
- You may sell builds under your own brand (`sell/README.md`), but legal, safety and product-liability compliance is the seller's job. Provided as-is without warranty. Straddling wheels vote (2026-11-19, later): the board now counts, on the balls whose contact crosses a revolution's edge at 1.5 ms, how many fit 1.5 ms better than an instant contact and how many worse, and sends both; when the sums say instant but that vote favours 1.5 ms by two or more, the Pi advises 1.5 ms. Simulated, held out with the rule written first: 71 of 120 spread contacts named against 58, no instant contact misadvised.
